{{RunningHeader|tenaculum|6228|tend}}2. In ''entom.'', the pair of microscopic chitinous processes on the under side of the abdomen of podurans or springtails, serving as a catch to hold the elater or springing-organ in place. ''A. S. Packard.'' ¶ '''tenacy†''' (ten′ạ̄-si), ''n.'' [< L. ''tenax'' (''tenac-'') (see ''tenacious'') + ''-y''3.] Tenacity; obstinacy. {{smaller block|Highest excellence is void of all envy, selfishness, and ''tenacy''. {{right|''Barrow'', Sermons, II. xii. (''Latham.'')}}}} '''tenail, tenaille''' (te-nāl′), ''n.'' [< F. ''tenaille'' = Pr. ''tenalha'' = Sp. ''tenaza'' = It. ''tanaglia'', < ML. *''tenacula'', f., orig. LL. neut. pl. of ''tenaculum'', a holder: see ''tenaculum''.] In ''fort.'', an outwork or rampart raised in the main ditch immediately in front of the curtain, between two bastions. {{smaller|In its simplest form it consists of two faces forming with each other a reëntering angle; but generally it consists of three faces forming two reëntering angles, in which case it is called a ''double tenail''. Any work belonging either to permanent or to field fortification which, on the plan, consists of a succession of lines forming salient and reëntering angles alternately, is said to be ''à tenaille''.}} '''tenaillon''' (te-nal′yon), ''n.'' [F.: see ''tenail''.] In ''fort.'', a work constructed on each side of the ravelins, like the lunettes, but differing in that one of the faces of the tenaillon is in the direction of the ravelin, whereas that of the lunette is perpendicular to it. Works of this kind are seldom adopted. '''tenancy''' (ten′an-si), ''n.'' [< OF. ''tenance'', possession, = Sp. Pg. ''tenencia'' = ML. ''tenentia'', < L. ''tenen(t-)s'', a tenant: see ''tenant''1.] 1. In ''law'': (''a'') A holding by private ownership; estate; tenure: as, ''tenancy'' in fee simple; ''tenancy'' in tail. (''b''†) A habitation or dwelling-place held of another. {{smaller block|The said John Scrips had in like sort divided a Tenement in Shordich into or about seventeene ''Tenancies'' or dwellings, and the same inhabited by divers persons. {{right|''Proc. in Star Chamber'', an. 40 Queen Elizabeth, quoted in [Ribton-Turner's Vagrants and Vagrancy, p. 123.}}}} 2. The period during which lands or tenements are held or occupied by a tenant.—'''Entire tenancy.''' {{smaller|See ''entire''.}}—'''Estate in joint tenancy.''' {{smaller|See ''estate''.}}—'''Several tenancy.''' {{smaller|See ''entire tenancy''.}}—'''Severance of a joint tenancy.''' {{smaller|See ''severance''.}}—'''Tenancy at will.''' {{smaller|See ''estate at will'', under ''estate''.}}—'''Tenancy by entireties.''' {{smaller|See ''entirety''.}}—'''Tenancy by the courtesy of England.''' {{smaller|See ''courtesy of England'', under ''courtesy''.}}—'''Tenancy from year to year,''' {{smaller|a tenancy which is implied by law sometimes, on the termination of a lease for a year or years and a continuance of the possession without a new agreement.}}—'''Tenancy in common,''' {{smaller|a holding in common with others; an estate consisting in a right to a share of an undivided thing; a tenancy in which all have or are entitled to a common or joint possession, but each has a separate or several title to his undivided share which he can dispose of without affecting the others: distinguished from ''joint tenancy''. See ''estate''. Sometimes called ''coparcenary''.}} '''tenant'''1 (ten′ant), ''n.'' [< ME. ''tenant'', ''tenaunt'', < OF. ''tenant'', a tenant, = Pg. It. ''tenente'', a lieutenant, < L. ''tenen(t-)s'', ppr. of ''tenere'', hold, keep, possess. Cf. ''lieutenant''. From the L. ''tenere'' are also ult. E. ''tenable'', ''tenacious'', ''tenacy'', tempt, temptation'', etc.] 1. In ''law'': (''a'') A person who holds real property by private ownership, by any kind of title, either in fee, for life, for years, or at will. {{smaller|The term is sometimes used in reference to interests in pure personalty, as when we speak of one as ''tenant'' for life of a fund.}} (''b'') More specifically, one who holds under a superior owner, as a lessee or occupant for rent: used thus as correlative to ''landlord''. {{smaller block|I have been your ''tenant'', and your father's ''tenant'', these fourscore years. {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 1. 14.}}}} {{smaller block|[The word always implies indirectly the existence of a paramount right, like that of a feudal lord or the modern right of eminent domain. States or nations are not spoken of as tenants of their own property; subjects and citizens are.]}} (''c'') A defendant in a real action. See ''action'', 8 (''b'').—2. One who has possession of any place; a dweller; an occupant. {{smaller block|Oh fields! Oh woods! when, when shall I be made The happy ''tenant'' of your shade? {{right|''Cowley'', The Wish.}}}} {{smaller block|The sheepfold here Pours out its fleecy ''tenants'' o'er the glebe. {{right|''Cowper'', Task, i. 291.}}}} 3. In ''her.'', same as ''supporter''. {{smaller|A distinction has been made between these terms by alleging that the tenant holds the shield as if keeping it upright, as is usual with modern supporters, but does not support its weight or lift it. (Compare ''supporter''.) Some writers, following the French heralds, use ''tenant'' for a human figure holding or flanking the shield, reserving ''supporter'' for an animal. Also ''tenent''.}}—'''Chief tenant.''' {{smaller|Same as ''tenant in capite''.}}—'''Customary tenant.''' {{smaller|See ''customary freehold'', under ''customary''.}}—'''Kindly tenant.''' {{smaller|See ''kindly''.}}—'''Landlord and Tenant Act.''' {{smaller|See ''landlord''.}}—'''Particular tenant.''' {{smaller|See ''particular''.}}—'''Sole tenant''', {{smaller|one who holds in his own sole}} right, and not with another.—'''Tenant at sufferance,''' one who, having been in lawful possession of land, keeps it after the title has come to an end without express agreement with the rightful owner.—'''Tenant at will,''' one in possession of lands who holds at the will of the lessor or owner.—'''Tenant by copy of court-roll,''' one who is {{smaller|admitted tenant of any lands, etc., within a manor.—'''Tenant by courtesy.''' See under ''courtesy.''—'''Tenant by the verge.''' See ''verge.''—'''Tenant for life, life tenant.''' See ''estate for life,'' under ''estate.''—'''Tenant in capite, tenant in chief.''' See ''in capite.''—'''Tenant in common,''' one who holds lands or chattels in common with another or other persons. See ''tenancy in common'' (under ''tenancy'') and ''estate in joint tenancy'' (under ''estate'').—'''Tenant in dower,''' a widow who possesses land, etc., by virtue of her dower.—'''Tenant pour auter vie.''' See ''auter vie.''—'''Tenants by entireties.''' See ''entirety.''—'''Tenant to the præcipe,''' the person to whom a tenant in tail granted an estate for the express purpose of being made defendant in proceedings to alienate the land by a recovery.}} '''tenant'''1 (ten′ạnt), ''v.'' [< ''tenant''1, ''n.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To hold or possess as a tenant; occupy. {{smaller block|The greatest part of Sir Roger's estate is ''tenanted'' by persons who have served himself or his ancestors. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 107.}} Goblins, to my notions, though they might ''tenant'' the dumb carcasses of beasts, could scarce covet shelter in the commonplace human form. {{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, xii.}} We bought the farm we ''tenanted'' before. {{right|''Tennyson'', The Brook.}}}} '''2†.''' To let out to tenants. {{smaller block|Three acres more he converted into a high way; . . . and the rest he ''tenanted'' out. {{right|''Strype'', Hen. VIII., an. 1530.}}}} '''II.†''' ''intrans.'' To live as a tenant; dwell. {{smaller block|In yonder tree he ''tenanteth'' alone. {{right|''Warren'', The Lily and the Bee, ii.}}}} '''tenant'''2† (ten′ạnt), ''n.'' and ''v.'' A corruption of ''tenon.'' {{smaller block|They be fastened or ''tenanted'' the one to the other. {{right|''Bp. Andrews'', Sermons, II. 81. (''Davies.'')}}}} '''tenantable''' (ten′ạn-tạ-bl), ''a.'' [< ''tenant''1 + ''-able.''] Being in a state of repair suitable for a tenant; that may be tenanted or occupied. {{smaller block|To apply the distinction to Colchester: all men beheld it as ''tenantable,'' full of fair houses; none as tenable in a hostile way for any long time against a great army. {{right|''Fuller'', Worthies, Essex, I. 544.}}}} {{smaller block|He even gave her permission to tenant the house in which she had lived with her husband, as long as it should be ''tenantable.'' {{right|''Scott'', Heart of Mid-Lothian, ix.}}}} '''tenantableness''' (ten′ạn-tạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state of being tenantable. '''tenant-farmer''' (ten′ạnt-fär″mėr), ''n.'' A farmer who is only a tenant, and not the owner of the farm he cultivates. {{smaller block|We may relieve this country from all responsibility, real or imaginary, for the misfortunes of the Irish ''tenant-farmers.'' {{right|''Nineteenth Century'', XXII. 729.}}}} '''tenant-farming''' (ten′ạnt-fär″ming), ''n.'' The occupying of a farm on lease, and not as owner. {{smaller block|''Tenant-farming'' is unprofitable. {{right|''Edinburgh Rev.'', CLXVI. 301.}}}} '''tenantless''' (ten′ạnt-les), ''a.'' [< ''tenant''1 + ''-less.''] Having no tenant; unoccupied; vacant; untenanted. {{smaller block|Leave not the mansion so long ''tenantless.'' {{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., v. 4. 8.}}}} '''tenant-right''' (ten′ạnt-rīt), ''a.'' '''1.''' The right of tenancy of a tenant on a manor, who holds not at the will of the lord but according to the custom of the manor. {{smaller block|The customary tenants enjoy the ancient custom called ''tenant-right:'' namely, "To have their messuages and tenements to them during their lives, and after their deceases to the eldest issues of their bodies lawfully begotten." {{right|''H. Hall'', Society in Elizabethan Age, App. I.}}}} 2. The right, or claim of right, in various forms or degrees, on the part of agricultural tenants, particularly in Great Britain and Ireland, to continue the tenancy so long as they pay the rent and act properly, to have the rent not raised so high as to destroy their interest, to be allowed to sell their interest on leaving to a purchaser acceptable to the landlord, and to receive a compensation from the landlord if turned off. {{smaller|The claim last mentioned, recognized as extending to crops left in the ground, labor in preparing the soil for the next crop, produce left on the farm, and of late years the value of permanent improvements, is that more especially known as ''tenant-right.''}} '''tenantry''' (ten′an-tri), ''n.''; pl. ''tenantries'' (-triz). [< ''tenant'' + ''-ry.''] 1. The condition of being a tenant; tenancy. {{smaller block|Tenants have taken new leases of their ''tenantries.'' {{right|''Bp. Ridley'', in Dr. Ridley's Life, p. 656. (''Latham.'')}}}} 2. The body of tenants; tenants collectively. {{smaller block|Yes, Mr. Huxter, yes; a happy ''tenantry'', its country's pride, will assemble in the baronial hall, where the beards will wag all. {{right|''Thackeray'', Pendennis, lxxv.}}}} '''tence†''', ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''tense''1. '''tench''' (tench), ''n.'' [< ME. ''tenche'', < OF. ''tenche'', F. ''tanche'' = Sp. Pg. ''tenca'' = It. ''tinca'', < LL. ''tinca'', ML. also ''tenca'', a tench.] A cyprinoid fish of Europe, ''Tinca vulgaris.'' {{smaller|It inhabits the streams and lakes of the European continent, and in England it is frequent in ornamental waters and ponds. The fish attains}} a length of from 10 to 12 inches. It has very small smooth scales. The color is generally a greenish-olive above, a light tint predominating below. It is very sluggish, inhabits bottom-waters, and feeds on refuse vegetable matter. It {{smaller block|is very tenacious of life, and may be conveyed alive in damp weeds for long distances. The flesh is somewhat coarse and insipid. The tench was formerly supposed to have some healing virtue in the touch. I. Walton ("Complete Angler," p. 175) says: "The Tench . . . is observed to be a Physician to other fishes, . . . and it is said that a Pike will neither devour nor hurt him, because the Pike, being sick or hurt by any accident, is cured by touching the Tench."}} [[File:century v08 p0032 c3f1.png|center|360px]] {{c|Tench (''Tinca vulgaris'').}} '''tench-weed''' (tench′wēd), ''n.'' The common pondweed, ''Potamogeton natans:'' so named from some association with the tench (according to Forby, from its coating of mucilage, supposed to be very agreeable to that fish). '''tend'''1 (tend), ''v.'' [< ME. *''tenden'', < OF. (and F.) ''tendre'', stretch, stretch out, hold forth, offer, tender, = Pr. ''tendre'' = Sp. Pg. ''tender'' = It. ''tendere'', < L. ''tendere'' (√ ''ten''), stretch, stretch out, extend, spread out, intr. direct one's course, aim, strive, go, tend, = Gr. τείνειν (√ τεν, ταν) = Skt. √ ''tan'', stretch: a root represented in Teut. by ''thin:'' see ''thin''1. From the L. ''tendere'' are also ult. E. ''tend''2, ''tender''2 (a doublet of ''tend''1), ''tender''3, ''tendon'', ''tense''2, ''tension'', ''tent''1, ''tent''3, ''tent''4, ''attend'', ''contend'', ''extend'', ''intend'', ''portend'', ''pretend'', ''superintend'', ''contention'', ''extension'', ''intention'', etc.; from the Gr., ''tone''1, ''tonic'', ''tune'', etc.] '''I.'''† ''trans.'' To reach out; offer; tender. {{smaller block|Then Cassivelaunus . . . sent Embassadour to Cæsar by Conius and Arras, ''tending'' unto him a surrendry. {{right|''Holland'', tr. of Camden, p. 37. (''Davies.'')}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To move or be directed, literally or figuratively; hold a course. {{smaller block|If I came alone in the quality of a private person, I must go on foot through the streets, and, because I was a person generally known, might be followed by some one or other, who would discover whither my private visit ''tended,'' besides that those in the inn must needs take notice of my coming in that manner. {{right|''Lord Herbert of Cherbury,'' Life (ed. Howells), p. 158.}}}} {{smaller block|See from above the bellying Clouds descend, And big with some new Wonder this Way ''tend.'' {{right|''Congreve,'' Semele, iii. 8.}}}} {{smaller block|I know not whither your insinuations would ''tend.'' {{right|''Sheridan,'' The Rivals, iii. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|It further illustrates a very important point, toward which the argument has been for some time ''tending.'' {{right|''J. Fiske,'' Evolutionist, p. 118.}}}} 2. To have a tendency to operate in some particular direction or way; have a bent or inclination to effective action in some particular direction; aim or serve more or less effectively and directly: commonly followed by an infinitive: as, exercise ''tends'' to strengthen the muscles. {{smaller block|By this time they were got to the Enchanted Ground, where the air naturally ''tended'' to make one drowsy. {{right|''Bunyan,'' Pilgrim's Progress, ii.}}}} {{smaller block|To make men governable in this manner, their precepts mainly ''tend'' to break a nationall spirit. {{right|''Milton,'' Reformation in Eng., ii.}}}} {{smaller block|No advantage was deemed unwarrantable which could ''tend'' to secure the victory. {{right|''Prescott,'' Ferd. and Isa., ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|Natural selection ''tends'' only to make each organic being as perfect as, or slightly more perfect than, the other inhabitants of the same country with which it has to struggle for existence. {{right|''Darwin,'' Origin of Species, p. 197.}}}} 3. To serve, contribute, or conduce in some degree or way; be influential in some direction, or in promoting some purpose or interest; have a more or less direct bearing or effect (upon something). {{smaller block|Farewell, poor swain! thou art not for my bend;
I must have quicker souls, whose words may ''tend''
To some free action. {{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, i. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|But the place doth not greatly ''tend'' unto tranquility. {{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 225.}}}} {{smaller block|All other men, who know what they ask, desire of God that thir doings may ''tend'' to his glory. {{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, viii.}}}} {{smaller block|The Spaniard hopes that one Day this Peace may ''tend'' to his Advantage more than all his Wars have done. {{right|''Howell'', Letters, iii. 1.}}}} {{smaller|=Syn. '''2.''' To incline, lean, verge, trend.—'''3.''' To conduce.}} '''tend'''2 (tend), ''v.'' [< ME. ''tenden''; by apheresis from ''attend.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To attend; wait upon as an assistant or protector; guard.
